messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Construction Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Vignette:
It was a Tuesday afternoon in late September when Mike watched his foreman, Dave, step backward onto the unguarded edge of the fourth-floor scaffolding. The sound Dave made—a short, surprised grunt—was followed by the wet, hollow crack of impact two seconds later. Mike had been holding a bundle of rebar about twelve feet away. He saw Dave’s hard hat tumble separately, saw the unnatural angle of his legs, and then he smelled it: the sharp, metallic tang of hydraulic fluid from a nearby jackhammer mixing with the heavier, sweeter smell of blood. That smell returned to him now, at random moments, unbidden. Sometimes it came with the taste of the coffee he’d been drinking that afternoon—bitter and slightly burnt—so that even a sip of morning coffee could drop him straight back onto that scaffold.

Mike is thirty-nine, divorced, and works a twenty-minute drive from the site where Dave died. He has been a laborer for seventeen years, but he has not set foot on a scaffolding higher than two feet since the accident. He told his new foreman he had developed a fear of heights, which was partly true, but the real problem was worse. It wasn’t just the height—it was the whole sensory replay. When he closed his eyes at night, he saw the image of Dave’s back arched in the air, frozen like a photograph. He could play that picture in his mind at will, and often could not stop it. The visual memory was so crisp that he sometimes caught himself scanning the faces of other workers, checking if they were also seeing it, as if the image had imprinted on the air around him.

What frightened Mike most was how the world had changed. Before, he had believed that if you were careful and followed safety protocols, you stayed alive. Dave had been careful. And now Mike was certain that no amount of care mattered. Bad things happened regardless, and he was powerless to stop them. That conviction settled into his chest like cold concrete. He began to feel that he was fundamentally inadequate—not just as a worker, but as a man, as a father, as someone who should have been able to prevent what happened or at least handle its aftermath better.

He never cried about it. He never let himself feel angry at the company for the missing guardrail, or at Dave for not looking, or at himself for freezing. Anger, he had decided, was a dangerous leak. If he let it out, something else might come with it—maybe the tears, maybe the screaming, maybe the whole collapse. So he kept his jaw tight and his voice flat. At home, that had been a problem. His ex-wife had said he was a ghost, unreachable. She was right. He came home from work, sat on the couch, and when the images pressed in, he learned to step out of his own body. He would focus on a spot on the wall and will himself numb, blank, absent. It was the only way to stop the smell and the taste from taking over.

He also found a second escape: gambling. Twice a week, he drove to the casino thirty miles out of town. He played blackjack for hours, losing small amounts, but the noise, the lights, the forced concentration on numbers and cards—it drowned out the pictures. It gave him something to feel besides dread. The gambling had cost him money he did not have, and he had started borrowing from a cousin, but he could not stop. The quiet moments were the dangerous ones.

Last month, his younger sister called. His daughter had asked why Daddy never came to her soccer games. Mike had made excuses—long shifts, bad traffic—but the truth was he could not bear to stand in the open, exposed, where anyone could fall, where the world could tilt in an instant. That call was what finally pushed him to walk into a clinic. He sat in the waiting room with his hands shaking, certain that no amount of talking could fix what was shattered inside him, but also unsure what else was left to try.
